Epigraphica Indica
------------------------------------------
Epigraphs or inscriptions, especially those of a permanent nature like stone edicts, are an important source of the history of a country. Tracing them, collecting the texts of the same and translating them into the current language is an arduous task. James Burgess (A.

-1916) who was the Director-General of Archaeology of the Government of India took the lead and brought out the first issue of a journal devoted to this, under the name Epigraphia Indica, in October 1888. Bound volumes of such issues were brought out later in 1892 and 1894.
Originally, inscriptions in Sanskrit, प्राकृत्, the Dravidian languages as also Arabic and Persian were brought out. Later on, it was decided to drop the last two from the purview of the issues.
The well-known epigraphist Hultzch (A.

-1927) who was the associate editor of this journal made some important changes in it. As per his suggestion it was brought out once in three months. One volume of eight such issues was published every two years. The first seven issues contained the texts of the inscriptions and the eighth, the index. The format too was changed.
The work has progressed fairly well. Till 1970, 36 volumes, containing more than 15,000 pages of material, have been published.
Sten Konow (A.

-1948) was the last European editor. After him many distinguished Indian scholars such as V. Venkiah, Hirananda Sastry, K. N. Dixit, N. C. Chakravarthy and B. C. Chabra have worked as editors.
Other scholars who have contributed to the journal’s development include John George Buhler (A.

-1908), D. R. Bhandar-kar, R. D. Bannerji, R. C. Majumdar, C. R. Krishnamacharlu and a host of others.
The journal, devoted entirely to the publication of inscriptions, has made a name for itself in the annals of Indological research.
Epigraphia Karnatika started in A.
-1927) in Mysore, under the aegis of the then Maharaja and Dewan also has carved out a distinguished place for itself.
